findings.title: Model configuration is selected on the test horizon with no validation split
findings.command:
grep -n -iE "valid|holdout|cross.?val" case_studies/smart_home/run.py || true; uv run --no-project python - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd
df=pd.read_csv('case_studies/smart_home/metrics.csv')
for ts,g in df.groupby('timeseries'):
    b=g.loc[g.mape.idxmin()]
    print(ts, 'n=',len(g), 'mape-best_rmse=',round(b.rmse,4), 'rmse_median=',round(g.rmse.median(),4), 'rmse_rank_pct=',round(100*(g.rmse<b.rmse).mean(),1))
PY
findings.expected: A validation split or inner cross-validation chooses the configuration; test_df is evaluated once for the final chosen configuration, and the selection provenance is recorded.
findings.observed: grep prints nothing (exit 1): there is no validation/holdout/cross-validation code. Line 192 computes metrics on test_df (ds >= 2016-04-01); lines 219-227 take argmin MAPE over all result rows per series. For each of the 5 series the MAPE-selected config is an extreme of 2592 test evaluations: Furnace 1 selected RMSE 0.0578 vs median 0.2775 (1.0th percentile), Furnace 2 0.0604 vs 0.2309 (2.7), Fridge 0.0134 vs 0.0163 (2.9), Wine cellar 0.0230 vs 0.0279 (7.4), Boston 3.7936 vs 3.4317 (86.3; MAPE and RMSE disagree).
findings.consequence: The reported best-per-series metrics are extrema of 2592 test-set evaluations, not held-out estimates. Vangja's 2592-config grid is selected on the same 260 test days used to compare against 17 classical models and the claimed Prophet/TimeSeers baselines, so the reported superiority is inflated by winner's curse and unequal search effort; no unbiased generalisation estimate exists.
evidence: Wine cellar [kW] n=2592 mape-best_rmse=0.0230 rmse_median=0.0279 rmse_rank_pct=7.4

findings.title: Reported Vangja table uses five different per-series configurations, not the documented single configuration
findings.command:
uv run --no-project python - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd
df=pd.read_csv('case_studies/smart_home/metrics.csv')
best=df.loc[df.groupby('timeseries').mape.idxmin()]
print(best[['timeseries','start_date','tune_method','tune_loss_factor','shrinkage_strength','intercept_sd','beta_sd','scaler','mape']].to_string(index=False))
print('distinct best configs:', len(best.drop(columns=['timeseries']).drop_duplicates()))
mask=((df.uniform_constant==True)&(df.tune_method=='prior_from_idata')&(df.tune_loss_factor==0)&(df.shrinkage_strength==1)&(df.intercept_sd==1.0)&(df.beta_sd==1.5)&(df.scaler=='minmax'))
print(df[mask].groupby('timeseries').mape.min().round(4).to_string())
PY
findings.expected: The paper's documented single best-performing Vangja configuration (flat trend N(0.5,1.0), beta_sd=1.5, shrinkage=1, UniformConstant active, prior_from_idata transfer, minmax scaler) should reproduce every Vangja row in the table, or the paper should enumerate the per-series configurations actually used.
findings.observed: The per-series MAPE-minimum selects 5 distinct configurations, differing in start_date (2013 vs 2015), tune_method (parametric vs prior_from_idata), shrinkage_strength (1 vs 100), intercept_sd (0.1/0.5/1.0), beta_sd (0.5/1.5) and scaler (maxabs/minmax). Applying the paper's documented configuration (UC=True, prior_from_idata, tlf=0, shs=1, intercept_sd=1.0, beta_sd=1.5, minmax) to all series gives MAPE minima over start dates of Fridge 0.1547, Furnace 1 0.8571, Furnace 2 0.3584, Wine cellar 0.3106, versus the paper's 0.1495/0.8518/0.3561/0.2498. Wine cellar is 24% worse than the reported value.
findings.consequence: The reported Vangja table is not the documented single configuration: each series uses a different test-selected config, and the documented config reproduces only Furnace 1 (and even there 0.8571 vs 0.8518). The paper's model-specification subsection therefore does not specify the model that produced three of the four reported rows, and the table cannot be reproduced from the documented configuration. This compounds the test-set selection in M-001.
evidence: 5 distinct per-series MAPE-best configs: Boston parametric/shs100/intercept1.0/beta0.5/maxabs; Fridge prior_from_idata/shs1/intercept1.0/beta0.5/minmax; Furnace 1 prior_from_idata/shs1/intercept1.0/beta1.5/minmax; Furnace 2 prior_from_idata/shs1/intercept0.5/beta0.5/minmax; Wine cellar parametric/shs1/intercept0.1/beta0.5/maxabs
documented-config MAPE minima over start dates: Boston 0.4171, Fridge 0.1547, Furnace 1 0.8571, Furnace 2 0.3584, Wine cellar 0.3106
paper Vangja table rows: Fridge 0.1495, Furnace 1 0.8518, Furnace 2 0.3561, Wine cellar 0.2498
Wine cellar gap: documented config 0.3106 vs reported 0.2498 (24% worse)

findings.title: Temperature-context arm is confounded with pooling and shrinkage, and no no-transfer arm exists
findings.command:
uv run --no-project python - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd
df=pd.read_csv('case_studies/smart_home/metrics.csv')
cfg=['start_date','use_temp_df','hierarchical','uniform_constant','tune_method','tune_loss_factor','shrinkage_strength','intercept_sd','beta_sd','scaler']
print(df.drop_duplicates(cfg).groupby(['use_temp_df','hierarchical','shrinkage_strength']).size().to_string())
print('tune_methods:',sorted(df.tune_method.unique()))
PY
nl -ba case_studies/smart_home/run.py | sed -n '92,112p;182,190p'
findings.expected: A factorial or one-at-a-time ablation that varies context-series inclusion, pooling type, shrinkage strength, and transfer method independently, including a no-transfer (tune_method=None) control.
findings.observed: Only two arms exist in all 2592 configs: use_temp_df='without_temp_df' occurs only with hierarchical='individual' and shrinkage_strength=0; use_temp_df='with_temp_df' occurs only with hierarchical='partial' and shrinkage_strength in {1,10,100,1000,10000}. No with-temp individual or without-temp partial cell exists. tune_method is only parametric or prior_from_idata, both transfer methods, and lines 188-189 pass the Boston model's t_scale_params and posterior idata unconditionally, including for the without_temp_df arm.
findings.consequence: The shipped grid cannot attribute differences to temperature context, pooling, or shrinkage: the 'with temperature' arm always also turns on partial pooling and positive shrinkage, and the 'without temperature' arm always also turns off pooling/shrinkage. There is no no-transfer arm at all (both tune_method values transfer the Boston posterior), so any claim that time-series context, hierarchical pooling, and posterior transfer were separately ablated is unsupported by the snapshot's only runner/artifact. The paper's ablation numbers cannot be produced by this grid.
evidence: with_temp_df / partial / shs=1:432, shs=10:432, shs=100:432, shs=1000:432, shs=10000:432
run.py:188-189 unconditionally passes t_scale_params and idata from temp_models for both arms

findings.title: Evaluation population includes the Boston context series and pools Celsius with kW, inflating aggregates 6.6x
findings.command:
uv run --no-project python - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd
df=pd.read_csv('case_studies/smart_home/metrics.csv')
print('series:',sorted(df.timeseries.unique()))
print('rows_per_series:',df.groupby('timeseries').size().to_dict())
print('mean_rmse_all5:',round(df.rmse.mean(),4))
print('mean_rmse_4appliances:',round(df[df.timeseries!='Boston'].rmse.mean(),4))
print('boston_mean_rmse:',round(df[df.timeseries=='Boston'].rmse.mean(),4))
print('ratio:',round(df.rmse.mean()/df[df.timeseries!='Boston'].rmse.mean(),2))
PY
findings.expected: Metrics are computed only over the 4 appliance target series (or the context series is reported separately and never pooled with kW targets), as the paper does for stocks by excluding the S&P 500 index from per-stock averages.
findings.observed: The artifact contains 5 series, each with 2592 rows: the 4 appliance targets plus the Boston temperature context series. run.py concatenates the Boston temperature frame with the appliance frame (line 44), metrics() loops over every group in test_df (utils.py:293-315), and run.py:222-225 iterates over all timeseries including Boston. Mean RMSE over all rows is 0.9042 vs 0.1363 over the 4 appliances (6.64x); Boston's mean RMSE is 3.9762 on a Celsius scale while the appliances are 0.013-0.264 kW.
findings.consequence: Any unweighted aggregate over the result table is dominated by the Boston context series rather than the 4 appliance targets: mean RMSE 0.9042 with Boston vs 0.1363 for the appliances (6.64x). The per-series winner loop also selects a 'best config for Boston', a covariate series, and the classical baseline summary covers only the 4 appliances, so the two sides of the comparison are computed over different populations and units (degrees C vs kW).

findings.title: MAPE selection is unstable on near-zero appliance series, and the paper's 8.5% improvement floor is actually 8.0%
findings.command:
uv run --no-project python - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd
df=pd.read_csv('case_studies/smart_home/metrics.csv')
print(df.groupby('timeseries').mape.agg(['min','median','mean','max']).round(3).to_string())
for ts in ['Furnace 1 [kW]','Furnace 2 [kW]']:
    g=df[df.timeseries==ts]; b=g.loc[g.mape.idxmin()]; r=g.loc[g.rmse.idxmin()]
    print(ts,'mape-best rmse=',round(b.rmse,4),'mape=',round(b.mape,4),'| rmse-best rmse=',round(r.rmse,4),'mape=',round(r.mape,4))
print('paper Furnace1 baseline->vangja improvement:',round(100*(0.9260-0.8518)/0.9260,2),'%')
PY
findings.expected: Use a zero-safe relative metric or MAE/RMSE for selection, report all metrics for the selected config, and state the true minimum improvement (8.0%, not 8.5%).
findings.observed: Furnace 1 MAPE has median 7.842, mean 7.361 and max 11.695 (i.e. 736%-1170% error); Furnace 2 median 2.656, max 4.383. The MAPE-selected configuration is not the RMSE-selected one for either series (Furnace 1 0.0578 vs 0.0548; Furnace 2 0.0604 vs 0.0577). The paper's table shows Furnace 1 classical baseline RMSE 0.0573 and MAE 0.0422, both better than Vangja's 0.0582/0.0430, while Vangja's only win is MAPE 0.8518 vs 0.9260. The paper's claimed improvement range 'from 8.5% (Fridge) to 25.9% (Wine cellar)' omits Furnace 1, whose arithmetic improvement is 8.01%.
findings.consequence: Selection by MAPE on series with near-zero daily values ranks configurations on unstable relative errors rather than forecast accuracy. The MAPE winner is not the RMSE winner for Furnace 1 (0.0578 vs 0.0548) or Furnace 2 (0.0604 vs 0.0577), so the reported 'best' configs are not best on absolute error. On Furnace 1 the classical baseline beats Vangja on RMSE (0.0573 vs 0.0582) and MAE (0.0422 vs 0.0430); the claimed uniform MAPE superiority is metric-selective. The paper's stated improvement floor of 8.5% is also arithmetically wrong: Furnace 1 is 8.01%, below the stated floor.
evidence: Furnace 1 mape-best rmse=0.0578 mape=0.8571 | rmse-best rmse=0.0548 mape=0.9465
Furnace 2 mape-best rmse=0.0604 mape=0.3552 | rmse-best rmse=0.0577 mape=0.3991
paper table Furnace 1: Baseline RMSE 0.0573 / MAE 0.0422; Vangja 0.0582 / 0.0430

findings.title: Temperature-regression baselines use realized future temperature while Vangja must forecast it
findings.command: sed -n '42,55p;255,272p' case_studies/smart_home/run_classical_baselines.py; echo '--- vangja runner ---'; sed -n '155,192p' case_studies/smart_home/run.py
findings.expected: Baselines and Vangja use identical information sets: either Vangja receives the realized test-period temperature as a known covariate, or the temperature regressions use only forecast temperature available at the cutoff. If future weather is assumed known, the protocol must say so and apply it symmetrically.
findings.observed: load_data() loads Boston temperature through 2017-01-01 (line 51), well past the 2016-04-01 train/test cutoff. fit_temp_regression builds X_test by merging the actual temp_df onto the 260 test dates (lines 269-272) and regresses on it. The Vangja runner trains only on data with ds < 2016-04-01 (build_dataset, lines 50-52) and then calls model.predict(horizon=365) (line 191), so its temperature series is a forecast, not an observed covariate.
findings.consequence: The temperature-regression baselines receive realized future temperature over the entire test horizon, while Vangja's with-temp model only observes temperature up to 2016-03-31 and must forecast the temperature series itself. The head-to-head comparison therefore changes both the model class and the information set: the baseline is an oracle-covariate model while Vangja is a genuine forecast. Any difference attributed to Vangja's Bayesian transfer versus the classical regression may be due to the baseline's future covariates.
evidence: run_classical_baselines.py:50-51 loads Boston temperature from 2016-01-01 to 2017-01-01
run_classical_baselines.py:257 merges temp_data on test dates; line 272 builds X_test with make_features(test_dates_range, temp_df)
run.py:155-156 uses tl_h_dfs[start_date] built by build_dataset, which keeps only ds < 2016-04-01
run.py:191 predicts 365 days forward for every series, including the temperature series

findings.title: Headline improvements have no uncertainty estimate or multiplicity control despite a 2592-config search
findings.command:
head -1 case_studies/smart_home/metrics.csv; grep -n -iE "seed|bootstrap|confidence|interval|std|repeat" case_studies/smart_home/run.py || true; uv run --no-project python - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd
df=pd.read_csv('case_studies/smart_home/metrics.csv')
print('columns:',list(df.columns))
cfg=['start_date','use_temp_df','hierarchical','uniform_constant','tune_method','tune_loss_factor','shrinkage_strength','intercept_sd','beta_sd','scaler']
print('n_configs:',len(df.drop_duplicates(cfg)))
print('n_series_x_configs:',df.timeseries.nunique()*len(df.drop_duplicates(cfg)))
print('any_std_or_ci_col:',any(c in df.columns for c in ['std','ci_low','ci_high','se']))
PY
findings.expected: Comparisons report uncertainty (posterior predictive intervals, repeated seeds/splits, paired tests) and control multiplicity for the 2592-config search, or the paper explicitly limits its claims to descriptive point estimates from one split.
findings.observed: Each configuration is fit once with method='mapx' and evaluated once on the single 91/260-day split. The result table has only point metrics (mse, rmse, mae, mape); there are no std/CI/SE columns. run.py contains no seed, bootstrap, confidence-interval, repeat, or paired-test code. The grid contains 2592 configs and 12,960 series-config evaluations before the 17 classical baselines and the claimed Prophet/TimeSeers runs.
findings.consequence: The headline claims (at least 27% over Prophet, at least 9% over TimeSeers, 8.5%-25.9% over the classical baseline) are single-run point differences computed after selecting extrema from 2592 configurations x 5 series = 12,960 test evaluations (plus 17 baselines), with no standard error, confidence interval, repeated split, seed replication, or multiplicity correction. A 9% gap on one series cannot be distinguished from run-to-run or selection noise, and the probability of a false winner grows with the search grid.

findings.title: Prophet baseline is a single default configuration while Vangja is a 2592-config grid search
findings.command:
sed -n '12,19p' case_studies/smart_home/run.py; uv run --no-project python - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd
df=pd.read_csv('case_studies/smart_home/metrics.csv')
cfg=['start_date','use_temp_df','hierarchical','uniform_constant','tune_method','tune_loss_factor','shrinkage_strength','intercept_sd','beta_sd','scaler']
print('vangja_configs=',len(df.drop_duplicates(cfg)))
cl=pd.read_csv('case_studies/smart_home/results_classical/classical_metrics.csv')
print('classical_models=',cl.model.nunique(),'classical_rows=',len(cl))
PY
grep -n "default configuration Prophet" /home/jovan/repos/vangja/paper/paper.tex
findings.expected: Baselines receive tuning effort comparable to Vangja (same search budget and the same validation/test protocol), or the paper reports a separately labelled untuned-Prophet comparison and does not attribute the gap to architecture alone.
findings.observed: The Vangja runner searches 2592 configurations (2 x 2 x 2 x 6 x 3 x 3 x 2 x 3), all selected on the test horizon. The paper describes the primary Prophet baseline as 'A default configuration Prophet model' (paper/paper.tex:650), i.e. one configuration, and the classical baseline artifact contains only 17 models / 68 series-model rows, each also selected per series on test MAPE.
findings.consequence: The headline improvements conflate model structure with search effort. Vangja is allowed 2592 configurations and the winner is chosen on the test MAPE, while the primary Prophet baseline is explicitly a single default configuration (and the classical family has only 17 model rows). A default Prophet on a 91-day series is likely under-tuned, so the reported 27%/77% gaps cannot be attributed to Vangja's transfer-learning design rather than to the 2592x larger search budget.

findings.title: The paper's Baseline row is a per-series test-selected oracle over 17 classical models, not a single baseline
findings.command:
uv run --no-project python - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd
df=pd.read_csv('case_studies/smart_home/results_classical/classical_metrics.csv')
best=df.loc[df.groupby('series').mape.idxmin()]
print(best[['series','model','rmse','mae','mape']].to_string(index=False))
print('models=',df.model.nunique(),'rows=',len(df),'distinct_baseline_models=',best.model.nunique())
PY
findings.expected: The 'Baseline' row identifies one named baseline method (or an explicitly labelled ensemble/oracle), and any model selection is done on a validation split rather than the test horizon.
findings.observed: Selecting the per-series argmin MAPE over the 17 classical models yields exactly the paper's 'Baseline' row: Temp Regression for Fridge (0.016033/0.011891/0.163297), Furnace 1 (0.057297/0.042241/0.926027) and Furnace 2 (0.073402/0.048607/0.446496), and Temp Only Regression for Wine cellar (0.034154/0.021916/0.337142). The paper's values are these rounded to four decimals. The 'Baseline' is thus a mixture of two model families, not one baseline.
findings.consequence: The paper's 'Baseline' row is not a baseline identity but a per-series oracle that chooses between two model families using the test labels. Its numbers are therefore optimistically selected, and the comparison is best-of-2592 Vangja vs best-of-17 classical on the same test horizon. The reported gap measures the relative search budgets and test-set selection, not the quality of a single deployable baseline.
